methods.method: Traditional cavity masonry (block+block, rendered) built by a client-managed 2+1 bricklayer gang on price-work/day rates, wet-plaster-free dry-lined fit-out; with a thin-joint aircrete Jumbo Blok (H+H Celcon/Ytong + Celfix 2-3mm mortar) variant assessed as a sub-option.
methods.how_it_works_here: Envelope take-off: GF 6.0x8.6m (51.6m2) + full FF over (51.6m2) + attic-truss crown storey (~45m2 usable) = ~150m2. Exposed perimeter GF+FF = 6.0+8.6+6.0 = 20.6m x ~5.4m = ~111m2 gross wall, ~89m2 net per leaf after openings, ~200m2 total blockwork both skins. Wall build-up for Part L: 100mm block outer leaf (medium-dense or 7.3N aircrete, rendered), 150mm full-fill Knauf DriTherm 32 cavity, 100mm aircrete inner leaf = U~0.17-0.18 at ~450mm finished thickness - flush GF/FF walls are trivial in masonry (the FF leaf simply continues off the GF leaf, no panel-alignment issue). Foundations: masonry is the HEAVIEST option here - within the 700mm tree's RPA the screw piles carry reinforced ground beams sized for ~2-3x timber-frame line loads (more/larger piles, deeper beams: budget +£3-5k vs the TF baseline; pile design must await the borehole); trench-fill on the non-RPA remainder; beam-and-block GF floor spans pile beams with no oversite dig in the RPA. Party-line flank against the neighbour's garage: blockwork laid overhand from inside own land off the GF scaffold lift, footing kept on own side (piled/eccentric ground beam at that flank), Party Wall Act notices for the line-of-junction and any piling within 3m/6m. Crown roof: attic trusses (hipped 41deg perimeter via girder/hip sets, flat centre) craned OR - given the busy-road/no-crane constraint - hand-set loose attic rafter/truss components; trusses at 5-10 day lead; EPDM to the flat centre (~28m2), plain-effect interlocking concrete tiles (Marley Edgemere/Redland plain-effect type) to ~75m2 of pitch, matching the planning drawings. Airtightness without wet plaster: continuous-ribbon dot-and-dab perimeter bedding + taped/jointed boards, or a cheap sand:cement/airtight parge coat (~£3-4/m2, the one small extra wet trade worth keeping) - no pressure test is mandated for extensions but reasonable provision applies. No crane, no fabricator lead time, no kit deposit: blocks arrive on any merchant wagon with a Moffett and are hand-loaded - the method that best fits this site's access constraints. THIN-JOINT VARIANT: Jumbo Bloks (610x270mm) + Celfix sets in ~10 min, storey-height in a day is a genuine manufacturer claim; best deployed as thin-joint INNER leaf + conventional 10mm-joint outer leaf (outer paces the build anyway once render is the finish), because rendered EXTERNAL aircrete thin-joint has a documented shrinkage-cracking history unless movement joints (~6m centres) and a mesh-reinforced basecoat thin-coat render system are specified - straight monocouche on aircrete is the classic failure. H+H's own position: material premium ~20-25%, labour saving offsets it, 'overall cost about the same' - so it buys ~2-3 weeks, not money.

methods.cost_shell_per_m2: ~GBP630-720/m2 weathertight shell (mid ~GBP660/m2 = GBP98k/150m2). Arithmetic basis (bottom-up, ex-VAT labour / merchant-price materials): demolition of existing rear addition GBP4k; foundations GBP14-20k (screw piles + RC ground beams in RPA ~GBP8-10k, trench-fill remainder GBP4-5k, masonry-load uplift included); beam-and-block GF floor GBP4.5k; blockwork materials GBP4.5k (200m2 leaf @ ~GBP19/m2 blended) + DriTherm 32 GBP1.4k + ties/DPC/mortar GBP1.2k + steels/lintels (8.6m rear opening, FF steels, party flank) GBP5.5k + gang labour GBP7.5k (price-work ~GBP26/m2 + daywork details); FF posi-joists+deck GBP4.8k; roof GBP22k (attic trusses GBP7.5k, carpentry GBP4.5k, EPDM 28m2 GBP2.5k, tiling 75m2 @GBP70 GBP5.3k, lead/fascia/gutters GBP2.2k); windows/doors GBP9k; silicone render on mesh basecoat 93m2 @GBP65 GBP6k (can trail watertight); scaffold GBP3.5k (longer hire than TF); plant/skips/welfare GBP3.5k; SE+Building Control+Party Wall GBP4k. Note: 'shell GBP1,200-1,700/m2' web benchmarks are contractor-led single-storey figures; this is direct-labour across three stacked levels, which is why the per-m2 falls.
methods.cost_finished_per_m2: GBP1,150-1,450/m2 to decorated, serviced, habitable (bottom-up mid ~GBP1,030/m2 before contingency/VAT drag - do not budget on that). EXCLUDES: kitchen units/appliances, floor coverings beyond screed/chipboard, alterations to the existing house beyond the structural tie-in, design fees, and land of course. Fit-out adds ~GBP52k: dot-and-dab + tape-and-joint ~450m2 @GBP22 (no skim, no wet plaster) GBP10k; GF insulation/screed GBP3.5k; electrics GBP7.5k; plumbing/heating (rads, extend boiler) GBP7k; bathroom+ensuite GBP5.5k; loft stairs GBP3.5k; doors/joinery GBP5k; rooflights GBP2.5k; decorating GBP4k; sundries GBP3k. VAT nuance: materials carry 20% VAT (~GBP70k of spend); labour-only sole traders are frequently unregistered - the direct-labour model's hidden discount. Add 10-15% contingency on top given borehole pending.
methods.cost_for_this_envelope: Shell (weathertight, rendered): ~GBP95-108k. Finished (decorated/serviced, exclusions as stated): ~GBP175-215k for the ~150m2 added, realistic mid-case ~GBP190k inc. contingency and VAT drag. Best-case flawless PM ~GBP160k; tail risk ~GBP230k if piling scope grows or trades churn.
methods.labour_model: Client PMs directly: one 2+1 brickie gang (2 layers + 1 hoddie/mixer) ~GBP550-650/day or, cheaper, price-work at ~GBP24-30/m2 blockwork (GBP5-7.5k for the ~200m2 here - always price-work masonry if cheapness beats speed); groundworker subcontract for demo/piles-attendance/trench-fill/beam-and-block (~3-4 weeks); carpenter pair for FF joists + attic trusses + roof (~4-5 weeks); then roof tiler, EPDM installer, render crew, window fitters, dry-liner (tape-and-joint), spark, plumber, decorator as sequential labour-only packages. Birmingham skill market: masonry is the city's DEEPEST trade pool - this is the method with the least scarcity risk; brickie day rates GBP220-280 sit below the national average. The exception is thin-joint: few Birmingham gangs know Celfix, most will price the unfamiliarity UP, eroding the theoretical saving - H+H offer training/starter support but that is PM time. PM burden is the highest of any method: ~15-20 trade packages, weekly cash-flow, sequencing the party-line flank, materials call-off (blocks/insulation/lintels arrive in ~8-10 wagon drops on a busy main road - book Moffett offloads before 9am school run). Client is not hands-on, so allow a labourer/site-tidy day rate or the site degrades.
methods.programme_weeks: 22-28 weeks total: demo + piles + foundations + GF floor 4-5 wks (borehole and pile design are the critical path NOW); masonry GF+FF 5-7 wks traditional (thin-joint inner leaf variant: 3-4 wks); FF joists + attic trusses + felt/batten/tile + EPDM 4-6 wks; WATERTIGHT at ~13-17 weeks; windows + render 2-3 wks (render can trail); dry fit-out 7-9 wks. Weather exposure: mortar and render are the only weather-sensitive trades; laying stops below ~3degC - a Sept-Oct masonry start is fine, a Dec start is not. This is 4-8 weeks slower to watertight than the open-panel TF baseline; the client has accepted that trade.
methods.compliance: Full-plans Building Regs application recommended (piles + party structure make building-notice risky) - Birmingham City Council BC or approved inspector. Structural sign-off: chartered SE designs piles/ground beams (post-borehole), steels over the 8.6m rear opening, party-flank foundation eccentricity, truss support; pile installer provides load test/torque records for BC. Part L 2021 extension path (elemental, no SAP needed): walls 0.18 (100+150 full-fill DriTherm 32+100 aircrete achieves ~0.17; thin-joint variant slightly better - 2-3mm joints nearly eliminate the ~6% mortar thermal-bridge area); floor 0.18 (beam-and-block + 100-150mm PIR); pitched roof slopes 0.15-0.18 (PIR between/under 41deg attic-truss rafters), flat centre 0.15 (PIR under EPDM); windows/doors max 1.4 W/m2K. No mandatory airtightness pressure test for extensions, but continuous-ribbon dabs or a parge coat needed as 'reasonable provision'. Party Wall Act 1996: line-of-junction and adjacent-excavation (3m/6m) notices re the neighbour's garage - budget surveyor fees, 2-month notice lead. BBA/certification: DriTherm full-fill and H+H thin-joint system both BBA-certified and NHBC-accepted - no certification gaps in this method.
methods.mortgageability: Best-in-class - this is the yardstick every other method is measured against. Cavity block-and-render with concrete foundations and tiled roof IS 'standard construction' in every mainstream lender's criteria; no valuation haircut, no specialist insurer, full Kings Heath comparable value retained. Thin-joint aircrete is likewise standard masonry (used by volume housebuilders, NHBC-accepted) - surveyors cannot even tell once rendered. Two disclosure points only: the EPDM flat crown centre (keep it under ~25-30% of roof plan and most insurers don't blink - here it is ~25%) and piled foundations (normal engineering response to trees, fine with SE certification on file). Keep the SE pack, BC completion certificate and pile records for resale.
methods.risks: 1) Borehole pending: if made ground/shrinkable clay is worse than assumed, pile count and ground-beam depth grow - masonry's weight amplifies this (the method's main structural penalty vs TF); hold 10-15% contingency until the SI lands. 2) Render cracking on aircrete outer leaf: mandate movement joints (~6m centres, incl. at the junction with the existing house), bed-joint reinforcement above/below openings, and a mesh basecoat + silicone thin-coat system - NOT straight monocouche; this is the single most common defect route for this build-up. 3) Gang quality variance: direct-labour brickwork quality tracks the gang, not a brand - get references from completed rendered work, agree line/level tolerances in writing. 4) Programme drift = scaffold hire drift (GBP800-1,500/wk beyond the inclusive period) and winter mortar stops. 5) Party-line sequencing: overhand laying is slower and the neighbour's garage roof needs protection - price it, don't discover it. 6) PM overload: 15-20 packages with weekly cash calls; the cheapness thesis fails if the client buys back time with a main contractor mid-build (that converts to ~+25-30% instantly). 7) Cold-bridge discipline at the flush GF/FF junction and lintels needs someone checking - no kit supplier is doing the thinking for you. 8) Thin-joint variant: crew scarcity in Birmingham can turn the labour saving negative; treat as opportunistic, not planned.
methods.verdict_vs_baseline: Baseline: 150m2 x GBP2,045/m2 = ~GBP307k finished. Masonry direct labour realistic mid-case ~GBP190k (GBP1,150-1,450/m2) = saving of roughly GBP90-130k (~30-40%), driven by: no frame-kit fabricator margin/deposit (~GBP40-60k of TF kit becomes ~GBP12-15k of commodity blocks/insulation/steel), no crane (which the site can't take anyway), Birmingham's cheap deep masonry labour pool, and price-work laying. What it costs: 4-8 extra weeks to watertight, ~+GBP3-5k heavier-structure penalty on the RPA piles, the highest PM burden of any method, and weather exposure on mortar/render. Since the client has explicitly said cheapness beats speed, traditional block+block rendered on price-work IS the sane cost floor for this envelope - materially cheaper is only reachable by cutting spec or legality, not method. The thin-joint jumbo variant buys back 2-3 weeks at roughly cost-neutral money and is worth pricing as an inner-leaf-only option, but it is a speed play, not a cheapness play.

methods.method: ICF (insulated concrete formwork): EPS interlocking forms (Nudura / BecoWallform / Polysteel; Durisol is dead — in administration, woodcrete line continued by Ecobrix/Isotex) stacked by a semi-skilled crew, braced, then pump-filled with C25/30 concrete in ~1.2m lifts. Walls arrive structural + insulated + render-ready in one operation; thin-coat silicone render goes straight onto the EPS.
methods.how_it_works_here: GF+FF external walls only (~20.6 lm exposed perimeter: 6.0m flank + 8.6m rear + 6.0m flank, x ~5.5m to wall plate = ~113 m2 gross wall) in ~300-350mm ICF with 150mm concrete core. The attic-truss crown storey is roof carpentry, not ICF — ICF stops at a timber wall plate anchor-bolted/wet-set into the top of the concrete core (standard Nudura detail), attic trusses (hipped 41 deg, flat EPDM centre) sit on it exactly as they would on blockwork, and hip corners take the same girder-truss loads because the core is monolithic RC. FF metal-web joists hang off a cast-in ledger or ICF hangers. Flush GF/FF walls are trivial in ICF — one continuous stack, no oversail. Party-line flank against the neighbour garage: you cannot strip bracing or render a face hard against the garage, so brace one-sided and cast that flank against a permanent cement-particle-board shutter with a compressible movement joint + flashing where the garage roof abuts; above the garage roofline the EPS gets mesh+render. Because it is within 1m of the boundary, Part B external-fire-spread rules bite — the rendered/boarded EPS face needs the system's fire-rated boundary detail (available in the BBA certs), and Party Wall Act s.6 notices for pile excavation within 3m of the garage. On the RPA side, screw piles + RC ring beam work, BUT be honest about weight: an ICF wall is ~2 t/lm line load at GF (vs ~0.5 t/lm timber frame), so the pile schedule gets denser/larger and the ring beam stiffer — budget +3-6k vs a TF ring beam, pending the borehole. Concrete arrives by line pump (£300-450/visit) so the busy-road/no-crane constraint is solved — but each of the 3-4 pours (~19 m3 total incl. waste) is a small part-load with minimum-load charges.

methods.labour_model: Genuinely PM-compatible but not genuinely unskilled: the stacking is semi-skilled (2 labourers at £120-150/day can do 5-10 m2/day after training), the POUR is the skill — lift heights, consolidation, plumb, blowout prevention. US/Canadian trade data is blunt: a crew on its fifth pour costs 1.5-2x in fixes vs an experienced one, and errors are locked in concrete. Right model for Vicarage Road: one experienced ICF setter/lead (£250-350/day, from ICF Midlands or Total ICF's network) + 2 labourers + supplier on site for first course and first pour day (Total ICF Birmingham trains free). Birmingham skill scarcity is moderate — two dedicated ICF outfits in the city is unusually good for the UK, but book the lead 6-8 weeks out. PM burden: high on the 3-4 pour days (pump booking, concrete slots, bracing checks, weather) and at the party-line shutter; low between pours. Not a "wet trade" in the plasterer/brickie sense, but it IS pumped wet concrete + wet render — if the client's minimum-wet-trades instinct is about drying time and trade dependency, ICF half-honours it (no blockwork, no wet plaster needed internally) and half-violates it (concrete is the structure).
methods.programme_weeks: 26-34 weeks to finished: demo + piles/ring beam 3-4; GF floor 1-2; ICF GF stack+pour 2-3; FF floor 1; ICF FF 2-3; wall plate + attic trusses + tile/EPDM 4-5; windows + render 3-4 (watertight at ~15-19 weeks with a novice-led crew — an experienced crew would shave 3-4 weeks, but cheapness beats speed here); first/second fix + finishes 10-14. Winter pours need frost precautions — sequence pours for Sep-Nov or spring.
methods.compliance: Full-plans Building Regs application recommended (party structure + piles). Structural sign-off: SE designs core thickness/rebar, lintel cores, girder-truss bearings, and the pile/ring-beam schedule from the pending borehole — every mainstream ICF supplier provides standard calc packages the SE adapts; £2-3.5k. Part L 2021 extension route: elemental U-values — walls 0.18 required, ICF delivers 0.18 down to 0.11 as-standard, roof 0.15 via attic-truss insulation, and system airtightness (3 m3/h.m2 or better achievable) gives headroom if a SAP whole-extension trade-off is needed for the glazed rear. Certification: use an ICFA-member system with a current BBA cert (Nudura, Beco, Polysteel all hold third-party certification; BBA cites 60+ year service life) — keep the cert, SE calcs and Building Control completion certificate in the property file. Part B boundary-face fire detail on the garage flank per the BBA cert. Party Wall Act: s.6 notices (piles within 3m of garage foundations); screw piles are low-vibration, which helps consent.
methods.mortgageability: Strong — this is ICF's cleanest win. The Council of Mortgage Lenders' valuation panel accepted ICF as a STANDARD form of construction in 2010, subject to valid third-party (BBA-type) certification and supply via an ICFA member (icfa.org.uk; confirmed by Thermohouse/Beco lender guidance). Rendered + tiled it is visually indistinguishable from masonry and matches the planning drawings. Critically, this is an extension to a 1930s brick detached, so the house's construction classification doesn't change on any lender questionnaire; no non-standard-construction haircut in a Kings Heath valuation. Insurers treat rendered ICF as standard once notified; use renovation/structural-works cover during the build. A 10-year structural warranty or PCC is only needed if selling/remortgaging soon — building-regs completion + retained certs suffices otherwise.
methods.risks: 1) Pour-day blowout or out-of-plumb walls with a novice crew — 1.5-2x fix cost multiplier is documented; mitigate with an experienced lead and manufacturer supervision of pour one. 2) Weight vs the RPA foundations: ~2 t/lm line loads (4x timber frame) mean more/bigger screw piles and a stiffer ring beam — the borehole could erode £3-6k of any saving; get the pile quote priced for ICF loads BEFORE committing. 3) Party-line flank is single-sided work: permanent shutter, no external render access behind the garage, fire-rated boundary detail on EPS — buildable but fiddly, and the worst place for a first-timer error. 4) Small-pour economics: 3-4 part-load pours with pump minimums erode the per-m2 quotes, which assume house-scale volumes. 5) Services must be pre-planned as cast-in conduits — late layout changes are expensive in concrete. 6) Supplier fragility: Durisol gone, Logix thin — spec only Nudura/Beco/Polysteel to protect the lender paper trail. 7) VAT 20% throughout. 8) Winter concrete. 9) It does not honour "minimum wet trades" in spirit — concrete and render are the method.
methods.verdict_vs_baseline: Baseline £2,045/m2 finished = ~£307k for 150 m2. ICF direct-labour lands ~£220-260k (£1,450-1,750/m2) — a saving of roughly £45-85k (£300-550/m2). BUT be clear where the saving comes from: NOT the walls. At £150-220/m2 installed, the ICF wall element is roughly cost-neutral against open-panel timber frame once concrete, pump visits and bracing hire are counted on a job this small; walls are only ~15-20% of project cost. The real savings are (a) thin-coat render straight onto EPS with no carrier board (£3-5k better than TF), (b) insulation + airtightness + render substrate arriving in one trade, deleting separate insulation and membrane packages, and (c) the same direct-labour finishing economics the baseline already assumes. The price paid: pour-day risk concentrated in 3-4 make-or-break days, a heavier structure that partly refunds itself to the piling contractor near the tree, and an awkward single-sided boundary flank. If the absolute legal floor on cost is the goal, PM-led cavity blockwork with Birmingham's plentiful bricklayers is likely £50-150/m2 cheaper still than ICF — but it is slower to watertight and maximises the wet trades the client dislikes. ICF is the credible middle: cheaper than the baseline, lender-clean, and buildable by a small semi-skilled gang, provided the client buys one experienced setter and prices the piles for concrete weight before signing anything.

methods.method: Light-gauge steel frame (LGSF) engineered kit, bought as close to the fabricator as possible (Frameclad, Hadley, U-Roof-type kit firms — NOT rollformers, see below), erected by a 2-man semi-skilled crew with no crane; warm-frame insulation outside the steel, render carrier board + through-coloured silicone render to match planning drawings.
methods.how_it_works_here: Demolish rear addition, then screw piles + galvanised cold-rolled steel ground-beam grillage (LGSF pairs naturally with helical piles because the superstructure is very light — smaller/fewer piles inside the 700mm tree's RPA, no-dig, low vibration next to the neighbour's garage on the party line). Fabricator supplies an engineered panelised kit: C-section loadbearing wall panels GF+FF (flush storeys are trivial in LGSF — same panel line both floors), lattice/joist floor cassettes, and the crown roof as either cold-rolled attic frames or (cheaper, recommended) timber attic trusses dropped onto the LGSF wall head — 41 deg hips tiled with plain-effect interlocking tiles, EPDM on the flat centre deck. Every component is stick/panel size, 2-man liftable — no crane on the busy main road, just a scaffold licence. Walls: 12mm sheathing + breather; Part L via hybrid warm-frame (mineral wool between studs + 60-80mm PIR/phenolic continuously OUTSIDE the sheathing — SCI rule: min ~33% of thermal resistance outside the steel to kill cold-bridging and interstitial condensation) hitting wall U=0.18, roof 0.15-0.16. Render carrier board (Aquapanel/Weather Defence class) on the external insulation, silicone render. Junction to the retained 1930s masonry via movement joints/beads; Party Wall Act s.1/s.6 notices for piles within 3m/6m of the garage.
supply_chain: Frameclad Ltd, Pensnett Trading Estate, Kingswinford, Dudley DY6 (~9 miles from Kings Heath) - designs, rollforms (Howick machines) and supplies loadbearing LGSF kits with in-house engineering; the most credible near-direct local source for a one-off ~150m2 kit; expect supply-only ~GBP 300-450/m2 GIFA incl. design/SE calcs (quote needed - no published domestic price list)
Hadley Group / HadleyFRAME, Smethwick B66 - BOPAS-accredited LGSF system, Birmingham-based, but volume-oriented; may decline a single extension or price it high

Voestalpine Metsec, Oldbury B69 - SFS/loadbearing sections but sells through fabricators/installers, not homeowner kits; benchmark only (SFS frame-only supplied+installed GBP 85-120/m2 WALL, +sheathing/membranes GBP 130-180/m2 wall - BAS Frames 2026 guide)

U-Roof Ltd - patented U-profile LGSF kits for domestic extensions and room-in-roof, explicitly no-crane, self-erect-friendly; published guide GBP 1,500-3,000/m2 for finished single-storey work, kit element materially less

SPJ Manufacturing - UK LGSF manufacturer, engineered supply-only kits
Springfield Steel Buildings, Hull - supply-only galvanised cold-rolled kits, free UK delivery, 6-8 week lead time

Render system: Knauf Aquapanel or Siniat Weather Defence carrier board ~GBP 26-35/m2 material (InsulationGo); through-coloured silicone render installed GBP 75-130/m2 (MyJobQuote/Kent Plasterers 2026)

Screw piles: GroundPlug UK / Paalupiste / regional helical installers - GBP 100-200/lm, single-storey extension packages GBP 8,000-18,000; two-storey LGSF loads still light, budget GBP 14,000-20,000 incl. steel ground beams
Labour benchmark: SFS/dryliner day rates ~GBP 190-230/day (2025 adverts); Birmingham has a commercial SFS labour pool (Metsec country) to draw from
methods.cost_shell_per_m2: GBP 850-1,050/m2 GIFA ex VAT (GBP 1,020-1,260 inc VAT) to weathertight. Arithmetic on 150m2: demo GBP 5k; screw piles + steel ground beams GBP 14-20k; LGSF kit supply-only delivered incl. engineering GBP 48-60k (GBP 320-400/m2 GIFA); erection 2-man crew 4-6 wks GBP 10-16k; sheathing/breather/external PIR GBP 8-10k; render board + silicone render ~117m2 wall @ GBP 95-115 = GBP 11-13.5k; roof coverings (EPDM centre + interlocking tiles on 41deg hips + RWG) GBP 10-12k; windows/doors GBP 9-12k; scaffold (main-road licence) + prelims GBP 9-12k. Total GBP 126-156k ex VAT.
methods.cost_finished_per_m2: GBP 1,550-1,900/m2 inc VAT to decorated, serviced, habitable — EXCLUDING kitchen and bathroom fit-out, knock-through/structural works inside the retained house, and professional fees (SE check, party wall surveyor, building control, arboriculturist). Adding kitchen/bathrooms (GBP 15-25k) and knock-through takes the realistic all-in to ~GBP 1,700-2,050/m2 — i.e. brackets the baseline. Basis: shell above + M&E first/second fix GBP 22-30k, board/skim GBP 13-17k, floor deck/screed GBP 7-9k, stairs to loft + internal doors/joinery GBP 8-12k, decoration GBP 5-7k, all + 20% VAT (no relief on domestic extensions).
methods.cost_for_this_envelope: Shell (weathertight) GBP 126-156k ex VAT (GBP 151-187k inc VAT). Finished ~GBP 233-285k inc VAT excluding kitchens/bathrooms and in-house works; ~GBP 255-310k genuinely all-in. Central all-in estimate ~GBP 280k vs baseline GBP 307k (150m2 x 2,045).
methods.labour_model: Fabricator delivers numbered, pre-punched panels + erection drawings; a 2-man semi-skilled crew (dryliner/SFS background ideal — Birmingham is Metsec/Hadley territory so commercial SFS installers exist, but LOADBEARING LGSF experience is thinner than carpentry) self-erects with tek guns, no crane, ~4-6 weeks for walls+floors+roof frames at ~GBP 190-230/day/man. Follow-on trades are conventional: roofer (tiles+EPDM), render contractor, window fitter, sparky/plumber, dryliner. PM burden on the client is HIGHER than the timber baseline: he must coordinate the kit design freeze (any change after fabrication is expensive), check the fabricator's SE calcs are adopted by his own engineer, police the warm-frame/thermal-break details (crews default to commercial SFS habits that fail Part L in dwellings), and sequence piles/beams to the fabricator's setting-out tolerance (+/-5mm — screw-pile heads must be surveyed before fabrication). First-time-crew error risk is the single biggest hidden cost.
methods.programme_weeks: 20-28 weeks on site to finished; weathertight in ~8-11 weeks from start (demo+piles 2-3 wks overlapping the 6-10 week kit design/fabrication lead; erection 4-6 wks; roof+windows 2-3 wks). Faster than masonry, similar to timber frame. Since cheapness now beats speed, note the speed advantage no longer buys anything unless finance costs matter.
methods.compliance: Full Plans Building Regs route recommended (LABC or private AI) so the LGSF details are approved before fabrication. Structural: fabricator's in-house engineers produce calcs to the Eurocodes/SCI methods (SCI P301; established systems are SCI-assessed, Hadley is BOPAS-accredited); have the project SE adopt/countersign them plus the pile/ground-beam design — this is the sign-off lenders and building control want. Part L 2021 new-extension elements: walls 0.18, pitched roof 0.15-0.16, floor 0.18, windows <=1.4 W/m2K — achievable with hybrid warm-frame per SCI P410/P411 (min ~1/3 of thermal resistance outside the steel + thermal-break detailing at openings); a condensation-risk analysis on the wall build-up is cheap insurance and worth commissioning. Airtightness: no mandatory test for an extension; taped sheathing gives good performance anyway. Render carrier boards (Aquapanel, Weather Defence) and mainstream silicone render systems carry BBA/ETA certification — keep certificates. Party Wall Act notices for piling within 3m/6m of the neighbour's garage; BS 5837 arboricultural method statement for pile installation in the RPA (screw piles are the accepted no-dig answer, subject to the pending borehole).
methods.mortgageability: Low risk done properly, but it needs paperwork. The property remains a 1930s brick detached — an extension does not normally reclassify it, and rendered LGSF is visually indistinguishable. Steel-framed HOUSES are treated as non-standard by many lenders, so the mitigation is documentation: building control completion certificate, adopted SE calcs, system certification (BOPAS/SCI/LABC warranty if available — Halifax/Nationwide/Santander accept MMC with NHBC/BOPAS/LABC cover), and photos of the build-up for the file. Tell the insurer; rebuild cost should come from a RICS reinstatement assessment (steel/MMC elements can cost 25%+ more to reinstate than brick). Residual risk: a cautious mortgage surveyor at resale flags 'part steel frame' and asks questions — the document pack answers them. Kings Heath value is preserved provided the render/tile appearance matches the approved drawings.
methods.risks: (1) Kit pricing risk: LGSF fabricators are geared to volume; a one-off 150m2 domestic kit carries GBP 3-6k of fixed design/engineering and can be quoted defensively — get 3+ quotes (Frameclad local, U-Roof, Steel Frame Buildings Ltd, SPJ, Springfield) and expect wide spread; 2026 guides put LGSF at an 8-15% shell PREMIUM over timber. (2) Crew inexperience: semi-skilled is not unskilled — wrong sequencing, missed noggins/bracing, or cut galvanising (site modification voids engineering and invites corrosion) are expensive; no site welding. (3) Part L/condensation failure if the warm-frame rule is fudged to save PIR — cold steel sweats. (4) Differential movement at the masonry junction cracking render — movement beads essential; GF render on a busy pavement-side elevation is impact-vulnerable (consider brick-slip plinth). (5) Acoustic: lightweight walls on a busy main road need double-boarding/mass — budget it. (6) Screw-pile feasibility hangs on the pending borehole; soft/obstructed Birmingham clay can force longer piles and eat the budget. (7) Scope-creep in comparing quotes — kit prices exclude sheathing, insulation, boards; compare like-for-like. (8) Change freeze after fabrication — design discipline required from a PM-client.
methods.verdict_vs_baseline: Not the cost floor. Central all-in ~GBP 280k vs GBP 307k baseline = saving ~GBP 15-30k (5-10%) in the good case, GBP 0 (parity) in the likely case, and a 5-10% OVERRUN if kit quotes come back at volume-averse pricing — because the steel frame itself is a premium product (2026 data: +8-15% on shell vs timber) and the baseline already strips main-contractor margin via direct labour. What LGSF genuinely buys here: lighter loads = cheaper/fewer screw piles in the RPA, zero crane on a constrained main-road site, dry fast erection, dimensional accuracy for the flush GF/FF walls, and a hedge against Birmingham carpenter availability. What it costs: higher PM burden, scarcer erection skill, warm-frame detailing discipline, and fabrication change-freeze. If cheapness truly beats speed, this method is a solid second choice, not the winner — it only beats the timber baseline if a local fabricator (Frameclad is 9 miles away) prices the kit keenly at ~GBP 320-350/m2 GIFA supply-only.

methods.method: IMPORTED TIMBER KITS — Polish/Baltic/Czech factory-made timber-frame panels (open or closed) shipped to Birmingham as a supply-only kit, erected by a local direct-labour carpentry gang; plus honest kill/keep on Alibaba flat-pack prefabs and shipping-container conversions.
methods.how_it_works_here: The envelope suits panelisation well: GF walls (three exposed sides, ~6.0m returns + 8.6m rear, ~56 m2 of panel), a full flush FF over (another ~60-70 m2 of panel), a 52 m2 FF floor as factory cassettes, and the crown roof done as attic trusses (41 deg hips, flat EPDM centre) — trusses are honestly better bought from a UK truss fabricator (they design to your exact hip/flat geometry and BS EN 1991 UK wind loads; importing trusses saves nothing). The kit sits on screw piles + steel/timber ring beam with a suspended GF cassette, which is exactly what the 700mm-tree RPA and BS 5837 want (no dig, low vibration next to the neighbour's garage; pile depths confirmed by the pending borehole). Party-line flank wall is built as a fire-rated panel (min. 30/60-min from inside, non-combustible outer face within 1m of boundary — cement render board or brick slip satisfies this) craned in from your side under a Party Wall Act notice. The realistic import play is CLOSED panels with factory-fitted insulation, membranes, airtightness taping and — crucially — factory-fitted windows at Baltic prices: that is where the saving actually lives, because it deletes UK window supply-and-fit and gets airtightness done in a factory instead of by wet-trade discipline on site. A laser survey of the existing rear elevation BEFORE design freeze is non-negotiable — 1930s walls are not plumb and panel tolerance is ±5mm. One artic (possibly two) delivers; a contract-lift mobile crane (~35-50t) offloads and erects in 3-5 days from the road with a temporary traffic management order on Vicarage Road.

methods.cost_shell_per_m2: ~GBP 700-1,050/m2 weathertight over ~150 m2 gross (incl. roof storey). Arithmetic: screw piles + ground-beam grillage + suspended GF cassette in RPA GBP 18-28k; imported closed-panel kit ex-works (walls, FF cassettes, membranes, factory windows) GBP 39-52k (EUR 45-60k at ~EUR 400-500/m2 over 103 m2 of GF+FF); UK attic-truss package GBP 6-9k; transport 1-2 artics + customs agent GBP 5-9k; UK SE adoption of Eurocode calcs + pile design GBP 4-7k; erection gang + contract lift + TM order GBP 14-21k; tiles ~75 m2 + EPDM centre ~25 m2 GBP 8-11k; render on carrier board ~120 m2 GBP 11-16k; scaffold GBP 4-6k = GBP 109-159k total, /150 m2 = GBP 727-1,060/m2. Excludes demolition of existing rear addition (GBP 5-8k) and VAT cashflow note below. For comparison, UK trade shell-only extension pricing is GBP 1,300-1,900/m2 ex VAT (with builder margin) — direct labour UK kit lands ~GBP 850-1,100/m2, so the import saves ~GBP 100-250/m2 at shell IF the Baltic quote is sharp.
methods.cost_finished_per_m2: ~GBP 1,450-1,800/m2 to decorated, serviced, habitable. Basis: shell GBP 727-1,060/m2 plus fit-out GBP 600-800/m2 (heating extension + UFH/rads, electrics, plumbing, skim/tape-and-joint on pre-boarded panels, loft stairs, flooring, internal doors, decoration, basic sanitaryware). EXCLUDES: kitchen units/appliances, landscaping, alterations to the existing house beyond the knock-through, demolition (add GBP 5-8k), professional fees for planning (already spent), and party wall surveyor costs (GBP 1-3k). All at 20% VAT — an extension is NOT zero-rated, and import VAT on the kit is payable at the border at the same 20%, so importing gives no VAT advantage, only a cashflow hit at customs.
methods.cost_for_this_envelope: Shell weathertight: GBP 109-159k. Finished habitable: ~GBP 220-270k for the ~150 m2 (i.e. GBP 1,450-1,800/m2). Central estimate ~GBP 240-250k finished if the Baltic closed-panel quote lands near EUR 450/m2 and nothing goes wrong in transit or at the interface with the old house.
methods.labour_model: Kit erection: one local carpentry gang of 3-4 (Birmingham has adequate timber-frame carpenters — the West Midlands feeds the Telford/Shropshire frame industry; not a scarce trade, unlike, say, ICF or CLT crews) for 2-4 weeks with crane support days 1-5, then the same gang does roof battening/tiling prep; separate roofing sub for tiles + EPDM (commodity trades locally); render crew for thin-coat on board (plentiful). Factory 'flying crews' from Estonia/Poland are offered but add travel/accommodation, CIS/CDM ambiguity and insurance questions — for one extension, a UK gang erecting to the factory's drawings is cheaper and cleaner. PM burden on the client is HIGH and this is the method's real cost: the client personally carries design freeze discipline, the laser survey, customs paperwork (EORI number, agent), currency hedging, stage payments to a foreign factory with little recourse, crane/TM booking, and the interface between foreign drawings and a local gang who has never seen that panel system. Budget the client's time honestly or add a GBP 5-10k UK 'kit coordinator'.
methods.programme_weeks: Elapsed ~28-38 weeks: design freeze + factory drawings 4-8 wks; fabrication slot 6-10 wks; transport ~1 wk — all overlapping demolition, borehole, pile design and piling on site (piles need the borehole result first anyway). On site: piles + ground beams 2-3 wks; erection to weathertight 3-5 wks from kit arrival (this method's one genuine speed win); fit-out 12-18 wks. Since the client has said cheapness beats speed, the long factory lead time is acceptable — but note it converts 'fast watertight' from a project property into a 4-week window that only opens after a ~4-month wait.
methods.compliance: Full Plans submission to Birmingham City Council building control (or a Registered Building Control Approver) — with a party structure, RPA foundations and an imported structural system, do NOT use a building notice. CE marking on the panels remains valid in Great Britain: the government extended recognition of CE marking for construction products indefinitely in September 2024 (Construction Products Reform Green Paper 2025 ongoing), so an EU factory's CE/DoP under EN 14732 (timber frame panel kits) or component CE (EN 14081 graded timber, EN 13986 wood panels) is acceptable to building control — UKCA is not required. The load-bearing calcs, however, must be localised: a UK chartered structural engineer must adopt/countersign the factory's Eurocode 5 calcs against the UK National Annexes (wind BS EN 1991-1-4 UK NA, disproportionate collapse Class 2A for the 3-storey-ish roof storey) and design the screw-pile/ring-beam interface and party-line junction — budget GBP 4-7k; agree this scope with building control at Full Plans stage so there is no late refusal. Part L 2021 extension U-values are comfortably met by a 140-184mm closed panel: walls 0.18, pitched roof 0.15, flat (EPDM) roof 0.15, floor 0.18, windows 1.4 W/m2K max / WER B — factory-fitted triple glazing from the Baltics typically beats this. No mandatory air test for an extension, but factory-taped closed panels give near-Passivhaus airtightness for free. Party Wall Act 1996 notices for the line-of-junction work at the neighbour's garage; BS 5837 arboricultural method statement + no-dig pile layout for the 700mm tree, finalised after the borehole.
methods.mortgageability: KEEP-grade outcome if detailed correctly. A rendered/tiled timber-frame extension to a 1930s brick detached is treated by mainstream lenders as standard construction — post-1970 timber frame with a recognised external finish is acceptable to virtually all high-street lenders (Strive Mortgages lender survey; Nationwide/TMW property criteria). The whole house keeps its Kings Heath valuation provided: (1) building regs completion certificate issued; (2) the render system is BBA/ETA-certified on its carrier board (or a masonry outer skin/brick slips are used) — uncertified render-on-frame is the one thing that makes surveyors write 'non-standard'; (3) a 10-year structural warranty (Build-Zone/Protek self-build extension policy, ~GBP 1.5-3k) or, minimum, a Professional Consultant's Certificate from the supervising SE — an imported kit has no NHBC-registered builder behind it, so buy the paper trail. BOPAS is irrelevant at extension scale; the warranty + completion certificate is what a future lender's surveyor asks for. Insurance during the build: non-negligent damage cover (JCT 21.2.1-type) given the party structure next door.
methods.risks: (1) The bespoke-extension problem: Baltic/Polish factories are cheap on CATALOGUE houses; a one-off 103 m2 extension tied into a wonky 1930s wall is a custom job and quotes can come back at UK prices — get 3 real quotes before committing to this route. (2) Currency and recourse: EUR-denominated stage payments to a foreign factory; if it goes wrong mid-fabrication your remedies are Estonian/Polish courts — hedge the FX and never pay more than 30-40% before loading. (3) Tolerance interface with the existing house — laser scan or the flush FF walls will not be flush. (4) Transit damage and a 6-10-week refabrication penalty for any wrong panel. (5) UK SE may require re-work of factory calcs (wind uplift on the 41-deg hips + flat centre is UK-NA-specific). (6) Crane day on a busy main road: TM order lead time and a rained-off contract lift costs GBP 2-3.5k to rebook. (7) Warranty gap if the client skips the structural warranty — hurts at resale. (8) Erector unfamiliarity with the specific panel system — pay the factory for a 2-day supervisor visit (~GBP 1.5-2.5k) at erection start. (9) VAT at import is a cashflow spike, not a saving. ALIBABA/CHINESE FLAT-PACK — KILL: USD 3-15k ex-works units + ~USD 4-8k/40ft shipping look tempting but have no CE/UKCA DoP, no EN 14081 strength-graded timber (building control can and does reject ungraded structure), sandwich-panel fabric at U~0.4-0.6 vs the required 0.18/0.15, no vapour-control strategy (interstitial condensation), and non-BS7671 electrics; making one compliant means rebuilding it, and bolting a non-compliant structure onto the house poisons the ENTIRE property's mortgageability. CONTAINERS — KILL for habitable space here: 2.39m internal width before 100-150mm of internal PIR (Part L) leaves ~2.1m rooms; steel cold-bridging drives condensation/corrosion; an 8.6m-wide plan means cutting away the structure you paid for; lenders class it non-standard (specialist lenders, bigger deposits, valuation haircut — the search evidence is unambiguous); and converted-to-habitable container space costs GBP 1,200-2,500/m2 anyway — no saving, all downside.
methods.verdict_vs_baseline: Baseline GBP 2,045/m2 finished = ~GBP 307k for 150 m2. Imported closed-panel kit realistically finishes at GBP 1,450-1,800/m2 = GBP 220-270k: a paper saving of GBP 40-85k, an honest risk-adjusted saving of GBP 25-50k (8-16%) — real but not transformational, and it is bought with ~4 months of factory lead time, EUR currency exposure, customs admin, and a high client-PM burden. The blunt truth the numbers force: the raw frame is NOT where the saving is — UK supply-only open-panel kit is already ~GBP 281-420/m2 (Fleming), and transport + SE adoption + import admin (GBP 9-16k) eats most of the Baltic factory-gate discount. The import only beats the existing open-panel-plus-direct-labour baseline when the closed-panel scope transfer is exploited fully: factory-fitted Baltic triple-glazed windows, factory airtightness, pre-boarded internals — deleting UK window packages and weeks of site labour. Recommendation: run a 3-quote shoot-out (2 Baltic closed-panel incl. windows vs 1 UK kit e.g. Telford) on identical drawings; proceed with import only if the landed closed-panel price incl. windows undercuts the UK kit + UK windows by >GBP 20k; otherwise the cheapness floor for this envelope is the current baseline executed with a supply-only UK kit and ruthless direct-labour procurement. Alibaba flat-pack: killed. Containers: killed.

methods.method: PORTAL/SHED HYBRID: hot-rolled steel portal/goalpost skeleton (barndominium logic) erected on the 6.0 x 8.6m footprint, infilled with insulated timber studwork, render-carrier board + silicone render outside, conventional attic-truss crown roof on top. Plus a numbers debunk of the polytunnel/steel-arch "live in it cheap" forum options.
methods.how_it_works_here: A true agricultural cold-rolled shed kit does NOT work for this envelope: ag kits are single-storey, carry no domestic intermediate floor (1.5 kN/m2 imposed + partitions), no heavy interlocking tile load at 41 degrees, and their cheapness lives in box-profile sheet cladding the planning drawings forbid. The buildable version is a bespoke two-storey hot-rolled goalpost/portal grid: 8-10 columns on the 51.6m2 footprint (party-line columns set in from the neighbour's garage with a cantilevered edge beam or padstone detail), steel floor beams carrying timber joists at FF, and a perimeter ring at wallplate level on which standard attic trusses form the 41-degree hipped crown with the EPDM flat centre - the roof is conventional either way, the portal saves nothing above eaves. Foundations: the portal concentrates load at columns, so screw-pile clusters (2-4 piles per column position) + steel or concrete ground beams - actually convenient in the 700mm tree's RPA (fewer penetrations, no-dig, Building Control-recognised), but pile design stays provisional until the borehole reports. Walls: 140mm timber stud infill between/over the steel, full-fill mineral wool + 50-60mm continuous external PIR or insulated render board to get U=0.18 and break the cold bridge where steel punches the insulation line; OSB + membrane + Cempanel/Aquapanel-type carrier + silicone thin-coat render for the planning-compliant rendered finish. Steel within 1m of the party line needs 30-60min intumescent/board fire protection (Part B). Net effect: you buy 5-8 tonnes of steel (£18-28k fabricated + erected) and then still build essentially the same insulated timber envelope, roof, render and windows as the open-panel baseline - the steel is additive cost, not substitutive, because everything the shed logic normally deletes (insulation, render, tiles, engineered founds) is a non-negotiable here.

methods.labour_model: Steel fabricator (design-fab-erect, 2-3 man erection crew + HIAB, 3-5 days on site); screw-pile specialist (1-2 days, machine-installed, no vibration next to the party garage); then a carpentry gang of 3-4 for infill walls, floors and roof; render sub; normal follow-on trades. West Midlands/Black Country has deep steel fabrication capacity so erectors are NOT scarce in Birmingham - but sub-10-tonne domestic portal jobs are unattractive to fabricators, so quotes will be sparse and dispersed; expect to chase 5-6 firms for 2-3 prices. PM burden is HIGHER than the timber-frame baseline: the client (not hands-on) must manage a steel/timber trade interface, tolerance clashes (steel erected to +/-5mm vs carpentry), thermal-bridge and fire-protection detailing, and an SE doing more hours (portal + pile caps + attic-truss bearings) - the opposite of the minimum-coordination brief.
methods.programme_weeks: Steel design + fabrication lead-in 4-8 weeks (overlaps demolition/piling). On site: demolition + piles 2 wks, steel erect 1 wk, floors + infill walls 3-4 wks, roof structure + tiling + EPDM 3 wks = watertight ~9-12 weeks; finished ~28-34 weeks. No real speed advantage over open-panel timber frame (panels also erect in 1-2 weeks), and the client has said cheapness beats speed anyway.
methods.compliance: Full Plans Building Regs submission (not building notice) given piles, steel and the party structure. SE sign-off required on portal frame, floor beams, ground beams and pile schedule - pile design provisional until the pending borehole. Part L 2021 route for extensions: new thermal elements at Table 4.2 - walls 0.18, roof 0.15, floor 0.18 W/m2K - achievable with 140mm full-fill + continuous external insulation, BUT steel penetrating the insulation line demands calculated psi-values/condensation risk analysis (BS 5250) or Building Control will query interstitial condensation on cold steel. Part B: structure and wall at the party line to the neighbour's garage needs fire resistance and limited unprotected areas; intumescent to R30/R60 on boundary steel. No BBA/UKCA issue for hot-rolled steel + timber infill per se (all conventional materials), but there is no certified 'system' - every junction is bespoke detailing, which is where regs risk and cost hide. Party Wall Act award required regardless of method.
methods.mortgageability: This is the method's second fatal problem. UK lenders class steel-framed dwellings as non-standard construction: specialist survey, some lenders decline, 20-25% deposits demanded of future buyers (Online Mortgage Advisor, Respect Mortgages, Intelligent Insurance). Modest goalpost steels inside an otherwise conventional extension are normal and invisible; but where ~150m2 - roughly half the finished house - is primary-structure steel portal with boarded render and no masonry outer leaf, a diligent valuer can describe mixed/non-standard construction, and buildings insurers ask the same question. That risks precisely the Kings Heath valuation haircut the brief forbids. The rendered appearance hides it from the street but not from a survey. A timber-frame extension with the same render finish is mainstream-standard construction; the steel variant buys risk for no saving.
methods.risks: 1) Cost risk: steel is additive not substitutive here - every pound of portal is a pound the timber baseline didn't need; 2026 steel prices rising £80-200/t (CBAM). 2) Valuation/insurance flag as non-standard at resale or remortgage. 3) Design risk: ag-style frames are not rated for domestic floors/heavy tile roofs - full bespoke SE design needed, eroding the 'kit' economy. 4) Interface risk: steel/timber tolerance clashes and cold-bridge/condensation defects are the classic failure mode of hybrid builds. 5) Borehole pending - pile numbers could grow under concentrated column loads in poor ground. 6) Party-line erection over the neighbour's garage: swing restrictions, Party Wall award delays. 7) Thin fabricator interest in a small domestic portal = quote and programme volatility. POLYTUNNEL DEBUNK (the forum option, killed by numbers): an 8.6m-span commercial polytunnel costs £3-6k, but single-skin polythene has U ~ 5.5-6.0 W/m2K vs the required 0.18/0.15 (30x worse), polythene film has no fire performance at a party boundary (Part B fail), hoops carry ~0.6 kN/m2 of snow and ZERO intermediate floor - a two-storey habitable structure is structurally impossible - and it is not the rendered, tiled building the planning permission describes, so building it is a breach on day one. Making it compliant means building a full insulated two-storey timber building inside the tunnel, i.e. paying twice; and no mainstream lender recognises it as a dwelling at all. US-style steel arch cabins (~$10k) have no UK certification route and the same planning/lender failures. Dead on arrival - the £3-6k buys nothing that counts.
methods.verdict_vs_baseline: Does NOT pencil. Finished cost ~£290-330k vs the £307k baseline - best case saves nothing material, central case COSTS £10-25k more (the £18-32k steel package minus perhaps £8-12k saved on loadbearing timber engineering), while adding mortgage/insurance risk, higher PM burden, and bespoke-detailing regs risk. The shed's economics depend on sheet cladding, no insulation and a slab - all three are barred by the planning condition, Part L and the RPA. The honest 'floor' for this envelope is not a structural switch at all: it is value-engineering the existing baseline (site-stick-built frame instead of a panel kit, direct-labour carpentry, standard attic trusses, one render package) which realistically lands £1,700-1,900/m2 - a £20-50k saving with none of the portal's downside. Recommend killing this beat and banking its one useful component: screw-pile clusters + ground beams for the RPA zone.

methods.method: THE MATERIALS + LABOUR FLOOR: ruthless direct-labour procurement regardless of frame — Birmingham 2026 price-work labour, sub-VAT-threshold labour-only trades (20% VAT never charged on labour), and bottom-channel materials (manufacturer seconds insulation, supply-only/seconds windows, ex-display kitchen, auction/surplus everything else). Finding: at the floor, the cheapest frame is NOT the timber-frame baseline — it is rendered cavity blockwork on price-work, because Birmingham masonry labour is the cheapest structural labour in the market (£17.50–20/m2 per skin price-work) and block + seconds-PIR is the cheapest legitimate Part L envelope. Open-panel TF embeds factory margin + VAT on the whole panel; blockwork lets you buy the labour VAT-free and the materials at commodity prices.
methods.how_it_works_here: Envelope: demolish rear addition (grab-lorry + labourers, £3–5k); screw piles through the RPA portion of the 6.0x8.6m footprint with SE-designed ring beam, conventional trenches outside it (piles £8–14k + groundworks/beams £4–6k — screw piling runs £100–300/m, a 6–10 pile extension £8–18k; budget 10–14 piles here as roughly half the footprint sits in the 8.4m-radius RPA of a 700mm stem); block-and-beam GF over the beams (£4–6k, no ground-bearing slab in the RPA). Superstructure: ~20.6m exposed perimeter x 2 flush storeys ≈ 180m2 of skins after openings — 100mm block inner + outer skin, full-fill seconds PIR cavity, thin-coat silicone render to match planning drawings. Masonry gang on price-work ~£12–15k labour, £6–8k materials. FF: engineered joists + deck £3–4.5k. Crown roof: attic-truss/cut hybrid (hips cut on site by chippies around a central flat zone — trusses hard to crane on a busy main road, cut roof needs no crane, only a beam hoist), timber £5–8k, chippie gang £6–8k, plain-effect interlocking concrete tiles supply-and-fit at the £55–85/m2 bottom of the range (~60m2 pitched ≈ £4.5–5.5k), EPDM centre ~18m2 £1.2–2k, leadwork/fascias £1.5–2.5k. Party-line side: blockwork built tight to the neighbour garage off the piled ring beam — Party Wall Act s.1/s.6 notices (piling within 3m/6m triggers the foundations notice); masonry is the easiest system to build hard against an occupied party structure because there is no panel-craneage over the boundary. Windows: supply-only budget uPVC casements from ~£200/unit (Wickes trade) or factory seconds — ~10 units £2.5–4.5k, fitted by the chippies. Scaffold £5–8k including highways pavement licence on the main road.

methods.cost_for_this_envelope: For the ~150m2 added/rebuilt: shell £75–105k (call it £90k central); finished £150–200k (central case ~£175k incl. fees, excl. contingency and client time). Ruthless-PM savings ledger vs paying a VAT-registered contractor for the same spec: VAT never charged on ~£75–90k of sub-threshold labour = £15–18k; contractor OH&P avoided = 17–25% of build; insulation seconds £2–3.5k; supply-only/seconds windows £3–5k; ex-display kitchen £5–8k; auction/surplus sundries £3–5k; price-work vs day-rate discipline £5–10k. Materials-channel + VAT items alone ≈ £30–50k of the gap.
methods.labour_model: Client as full-time coordinator (not hands-on), sequential trade packages on price-work wherever possible: groundworks gang (2, ~3 wks) → piling subcontractor (design-and-install, 3–5 days on site) → masonry gang 2 brickies + labourer (Birmingham 2026: brickie £220–280/day, labourer £120–160/day, gang ~£560–700/day, but buy it as price-work: £17.50–20/m2 blockwork, £400–700/1000 bricks) ~4–5 wks → chippie pair (£180–280/day each) for floors, roof, windows, second fix → price-work tiler → EPDM installer (1–2 days) → spark (£230–320/day) and plumber (£220–300/day) first/second fix → render gang and plasterers on m2 rates. Peak on site: 4–5 bodies. Birmingham scarcity 2026: brickies genuinely tight (housebuilding demand — book the gang 6–8 weeks out and never let them stand idle waiting for materials, which is the PM's whole job); sparks tight; groundworkers and plasterers available. CIS: a private homeowner engaging trades directly is NOT a CIS contractor — no deductions, no scheme registration; each trade invoices gross and handles their own tax. Every trade must genuinely be a separate self-employed business below the £90k VAT threshold for their labour to be VAT-free — verify status in writing; artificially splitting one builder's contract to dodge VAT is evasion, separate genuine trades is not. CAUTION: if these works run through Candor Housing (a business) rather than the client personally, both the CIS position and VAT treatment change — take specific advice before contracting that way.
methods.programme_weeks: 28–36 weeks (demo + piles 3–4; shell to watertight 12–15; first fix/plaster/second fix/decorate 13–17). That is 8–12 weeks slower than a driven timber-frame programme and 10–15% longer than a main-contractor build — the accepted price of cheapness-beats-speed. Winter masonry risk if the shell phase lands Nov–Feb (frost stops bricklaying; programme the shell for spring/summer 2027 if starting after the borehole).
methods.compliance: Full Plans Building Regs application (not building notice — you want conditioned approval before committing to seconds materials and pile design, and lenders like the paper trail). Part L 2021 new thermal elements in extensions: walls 0.18, floor 0.18, roof 0.15 W/m2K, windows ≤1.4/Band B — met by 100mm full-fill PIR cavity, 150mm PIR over block-and-beam, and 120–150mm PIR between/under crown-roof rafters. Seconds PIR is genuine Kingspan/Celotex production stock with cosmetic damage — declared lambda and certification are the manufacturer's own, so building control accept it; keep the datasheets and delivery notes because some inspectors ask, and a handful of BCOs are sniffy about unbranded facings — resolve before ordering. Structural: SE package (ring beam, steels, roof) + pile contractor's own engineered design tied to the pending borehole; SE inspection at each stage for the completion certificate. Airtightness: wet-plastered blockwork is inherently the best airtightness strategy at this price point (parge/skim = the air barrier). Party Wall Act notices both sides where relevant; s.6 foundations notice for piling within 3m/6m of the neighbour garage. No BBA/UKCA issues — every component is mainstream.
methods.mortgageability: The strongest of any method: rendered cavity blockwork IS the lender definition of standard construction — no valuation haircut, no insurer questions, indistinguishable from the housing stock Kings Heath surveyors price every week. Seconds/ex-display materials have zero effect on classification. The one gap: no main contractor means no insurance-backed guarantee — for a future remortgage/sale the Building Regs completion certificate normally suffices, but buy a retrospective self-build/PCC warranty or architect's/SE's certificate (£1.5–3k) if belt-and-braces is wanted. Site insurance: client must carry self-build/renovation insurance (contract works + public liability) for the duration since no contractor's policy exists.
methods.risks: 1) PM key-person risk: 20–30 hrs/wk for 7–9 months; if the client under-invests, the floor price evaporates through idle trades and resequencing. 2) No single point of liability — latent defects land on the client; mitigate with SE inspections and a bought warranty. 3) CDM 2015: with no principal contractor appointed, coordination duties effectively sit with whoever controls the work — appoint the lead trade as PC in writing per phase. 4) Seconds/auction supply is opportunistic: buy insulation, windows and kitchen months ahead and store (secure container ~£150/month) or the programme buys retail at retail prices. 5) VAT structure must be genuine (see labour model) — HMRC treats artificial contract-splitting as evasion. 6) Piling next to the neighbour garage: vibration/heave claims — screw piles are low-vibration (that is why they were chosen) but photograph-condition-survey the garage first. 7) Borehole could worsen the pile design (deeper/more piles, +£3–6k). 8) Winter masonry weather risk. 9) Price-work quality risk on blockwork — agree NHBC-standard tolerances in the price and hold 5% retention per package. 10) Overrun norm: self-managed jobs run 10–15% long; carry 10% cost contingency the floor figures exclude.
methods.verdict_vs_baseline: Baseline (open-panel TF + direct labour, £2,045/m2) prices this envelope at ~£307k for 150m2. The materials+labour floor lands at £150–200k finished (£1,000–1,350/m2) — a saving of £105–155k, of which roughly £15–18k is VAT legitimately never charged on sub-threshold labour, £30–50k is materials-channel + price-work discipline, and the rest is the gap between a padded TF direct-labour budget and true bottom-of-market masonry procurement. What it costs: 8–12 extra weeks of programme, 7–9 months of the client's working week, acceptance of wet trades (the one stated preference that must be sacrificed — blockwork + wet plaster IS the floor; a dry-trades floor via TF gives back ~£15–25k of the saving), full latent-defect and coordination risk, and zero slack for a passive PM. If the client will genuinely run it like a contractor, this is the legal and financial floor; if not, budget the middle of the band and keep the contingency.

methods.method: THE COMPLIANCE FLOOR — minimum legal/financial spec audit for a 2026 English extension of this size, used to floor-check every other method's numbers. Not a construction system itself: it defines what no method may omit and what soft costs are irreducible.
methods.how_it_works_here: FABRIC (Part L 2021, ADL Vol.1 'work to existing dwellings', Table 4.2 — these are the EXACT minima, not 0.26): new walls U<=0.18 W/m2K, new floor <=0.18, new roof <=0.15 (applies to both the 41-degree tiled slopes at rafter level AND the flat EPDM crown centre), windows/doors <=1.4 (or WER Band B), rooflights <=2.2. Trade-offs via area-weighted U-value or whole-dwelling SAP are allowed but new elements can never be worse than the limiting backstops, so in practice budget ~140mm PIR (or 90mm PIR + insulated plasterboard) in the timber-frame walls, ~150mm PIR above deck on the flat crown, full insulated rafter build-up on the slopes, and 25mm+100mm floor PIR. AIRTIGHTNESS: no pressure test is required for a domestic extension (L1B/ADL1 position confirmed by LABC) — only 'continuity of insulation and airtightness' workmanship, so £0 testing cost; the 8 m3/h.m2 new-dwelling target does NOT bind here. GLAZING: keep total glazed area <=25% of extension floor area PLUS the area of openings removed (the big demolished rear addition's doors/windows count toward the allowance — generous here); exceed it and you buy a SAP trade-off calc (~£150-£400) plus probably better glass. PART O: does not apply to extensions of existing dwellings — £0. FIRE (the big one for THIS envelope): GF + full FF + habitable attic-truss loft = a THREE-STOREY dwellinghouse with top floor >4.5m above ground. ADB Vol.1 then mandates a 30-minute protected stairway from the loft storey to a final exit (or to two separated ground-level routes), fire doors (FD20 min, FD30s20 in practice) to every habitable room opening onto the stair on ALL storeys including the existing 1930s house, full 30-minute (not 'modified') fire resistance to the new floor structures, and mains-interlinked smoke alarms on every storey (BS 5839-6). An open-plan ground floor through which the stair passes is only achievable with a sprinkler/watermist system plus a fire-resisting partition arrangement (~£3,500-£6,000) — if the design keeps a hall/lobby, that cost vanishes. Escape windows alone are NOT a lawful strategy above 4.5m. PARTY LINE: the flank wall abutting the neighbour's garage is within 1m of the boundary, so it needs 30-min fire resistance from both sides and near-zero unprotected (glazed) area on that elevation — render over any frame type satisfies the surface but the build-up must carry the rating. CEILING HEIGHTS: England has NO legal minimum habitable ceiling height — the attic storey is lawful at any height; the only hard geometry is Part K stair headroom: 2.0m generally, relaxed for loft stairs to 1.9m centre/1.8m at the edge. (Below ~2.2m over the bulk of the loft it will still be marketed/valued as 'restricted head height' — a value issue, not a legal one.) The crown-roof flat centre is precisely what makes this storey work legally at 41-degree hips. FOUNDATIONS/STRUCTURE: near the 700mm tree, building control will not accept shallow strips inside the RPA — NHBC 4.2-style depth tables in shrinkable Midlands clay would demand very deep trenches anyway, so screw piles/ground beams are effectively MANDATORY on that part of the footprint, not a luxury: full SE package (steel, ground beams, wind/disproportionate-collapse checks on 3 storeys of timber frame), pile design by the piling contractor's engineer counter-signed by the SE, and the pending borehole/soil report are all conditions of structural sign-off. Attic trusses come with fabricator's design certification (free within the truss package) but the SE must design the supporting structure. CIL: THIS EXTENSION EXCEEDS 100m2 GIA so it is CIL-liable in Birmingham in principle; the residential-extension/self-build exemption reduces it to £0 ONLY if Form 9 (exemption claim) is submitted and assumed liability + commencement notice are lodged BEFORE any work starts. Miss the sequence and the levy (2016 rate £69/m2, indexed well above £100/m2 by 2026 in charged zones, ~£15k+ on 150m2) becomes payable with no appeal. PARTY WALL ACT: two notice types are unavoidable — s.6 (excavation/piling within 3m of the neighbour's garage foundations, 1 month notice) and s.1/s.2 for the new wall up to/astride the line and works to the party structure (2 months notice). Consent in writing costs ~£0-£300; dissent means surveyors (£700-£1,400 agreed; £2,000-£3,000+ two-surveyor). The Act cannot be contracted out of.

methods.cost_shell_per_m2: This beat sets a FLOOR, not a price: for this specific envelope the legally irreducible shell content (Part L fabric ~£38-£55/m2 of floor area in insulation alone at 2026 PIR prices; engineered foundations over ~40% of footprint; 30-min floors; boundary-wall fire build-up) means no honest weathertight-shell quote can sit below roughly £900-£1,100/m2 in the West Midlands in 2026. Whole-envelope floor-check: shell ~£135k-£165k (150m2 x £900-£1,100); finished ~£205k-£233k (150m2 x £1,350-£1,550) vs the £2,045/m2 baseline's ~£307k.
methods.labour_model: Compliance is a certification chain, not a gang: BC surveyor (5-8 statutory inspection points: excavation/piles, DPC, structure pre-cover, insulation, drains, completion), SE (design + pile counter-sign + any lender/PCC inspections), truss fabricator's engineer (attic trusses, free in package), piling contractor's designer, party wall surveyor(s), Part P-registered electrician (self-certifies incl. interlinked alarms), Gas Safe for any boiler work, FENSA/CERTASS or BC for windows. None of these are scarce in Birmingham. The PM burden falls on the client and is real: sequencing party-wall notices (2 months before touching the line), CIL Form 9 + commencement notice BEFORE any ground-breaking, booking inspections, and collecting every certificate (completion cert, electrical, alarms, FENSA, pile records, SE letters) into a sale-ready pack — that pack IS the mortgageability of the finished house. Skill scarcity is nil; sequencing discipline is the whole job.
methods.programme_weeks: Statutory runway BEFORE ground-breaking: party wall notices 4-8 weeks (s.6 = 1 month, s.1/s.2 = 2 months, can run concurrently with design), BC full-plans approval 5-8 weeks (build can lawfully start on deposit of plans but full-plans approval is cheap insurance next to an occupied party structure), CIL exemption + commencement notice ~2 weeks admin, borehole + pile design 3-4 weeks. Net: ~8-10 weeks of paper ahead of the dig, largely parallelisable with procurement. During the build, inspections add zero duration; completion certificate 1-2 weeks after final inspection. Compliance adds calendar runway, not build weeks — consistent with cheapness-beats-speed.
methods.compliance: Route: Full Plans application to Birmingham BC or a private Registered Building Control Approver (post-Building Safety Act, functionally similar cost for domestic). Part L path: elemental compliance — Table 4.2 U-values (walls 0.18 / floor 0.18 / roofs 0.15 / glazing 1.4) + glazing <=25% of extension floor area (plus credit for the demolished addition's openings) = NO SAP calc, NO air test, NO EPC required; exceed glazing allowance and a whole-dwelling SAP trade-off (~£150-£400) is the fallback. Consequential improvements do not apply (<1000m2 building). Structural cert: SE calcs + borehole-backed pile design are a hard condition of approval near the RPA; attic-truss design certification comes from the fabricator. Fire: three-storey protected-stair strategy must be ON THE BC DRAWINGS from day one — retrofitting it is the classic budget-killer. Products: use CE/UKCA-marked or BBA-certified insulation, membranes and EPDM (standard brands all hold BBA certs — no issue, but an off-brand uncertified EPDM or recycled insulation with no declared lambda will fail BC and taint the file). MONEY LEGALLY CANNOT BE CUT from: the fabric U-values, the protected stair + FD doors + interlinked alarms + 30-min floors, the boundary-wall fire rating, engineered foundations near the tree, the party wall process, Part P/Gas Safe certification, ventilation (Part F background + wet-room extract), safety glazing (Part K), drainage (Part H), and the CIL paperwork sequence. Everything else — finishes, glazing quantity, heating spec above minimum, warranty — is discretionary.
methods.mortgageability: An EXTENSION to an existing 1930s house is not underwritten like a new build: no lender warranty requirement bites at drawdown unless the client is staging finance against the works. Legal minimum for future sale/remortgage = Building Regs COMPLETION CERTIFICATE plus the certificate pack (electrical, FENSA, alarms) — for most mainstream lenders that suffices for an extension. Caveats: (1) some buyers' lenders/conveyancers within 10 years of large structural works ask for a 10-yr warranty or a Professional Consultant's Certificate — cheapest hedge is a PCC from the inspecting SE/architect (low £1,000s, needs their PII) or an extension warranty bought BEFORE start (quote-only, typically low-£1,000s; retrospective ones run £10k+ and some lenders refuse them); (2) construction type: rendered timber frame with a masonry-appearance finish and a tiled crown roof is 'standard construction' to mainstream lenders PROVIDED the flat EPDM area stays a minority of the roof plan (most lenders tolerate flat roof <50% of area; the tiled 41-degree perimeter keeps this comfortably onside) — no valuation haircut expected in Kings Heath; (3) keep pile design records — ground-stability questions on resale near a large tree are answered by the geotech report, not assurances. Verdict: mortgageable at Kings Heath money if, and only if, the paper trail is complete.
methods.risks: 1) CIL sequencing: start any work before the exemption claim + commencement notice are acknowledged and ~£15k+ becomes legally payable — the single largest pure-paperwork risk on this job. 2) Fire strategy discovered late: pricing the loft as 'storage' then fitting it out makes the house three-storey retroactively; the protected stair must be designed in now, and an open-plan GF adds £3.5-6k sprinkler/mist money. 3) Borehole surprises: shrinkable clay + 700mm tree could push pile depths/count up; hold a £5-8k contingency on foundations. 4) Party wall dissent from the garage neighbour turns £300 into £3,000 and can slow start (but not stop it). 5) Skipping the warranty/PCC to save £1-2k is rational ONLY if the client can tolerate a possible retrospective £10k+ or a slower sale within 10 years. 6) Over-glazing drift during design pushes into SAP territory and better-spec glass. 7) Using uncertified budget materials (no BBA/UKCA, no declared performance) voids BC sign-off and the insurance file — the cheapest lawful material is the cheapest CERTIFIED material. 8) 'Restricted head height' loft (<2.2m over most of the floor) is legal but valuers may not count it as a full storey — protect the crown-roof flat area in any value-engineering.
methods.verdict_vs_baseline: The compliance floor does not itself save money — it caps how much anyone else's method can claim to save. Against the £2,045/m2 (~£307k) baseline: irreducible soft/compliance costs are only ~£6-11k, so virtually all saving must come from superstructure, labour and finishes, and the honest finished floor for this envelope is ~£1,350-£1,550/m2 (~£205-233k) — a maximum lawful saving of roughly £75-100k versus baseline, bought with heavy client PM, basic finishes and calendar (not build) time for the 8-10 week statutory runway. Floor-check rule for the other researchers: reject any shell figure under ~£900/m2 or finished figure under ~£1,300/m2, any scheme without a protected stair to the loft, any strip-footing assumption inside the RPA, and any programme that starts digging inside the party-wall/CIL notice windows. Cheapness beats speed is compatible with this floor; cheapness beating legality is not available.
